questions.title: What is the main motivation behind replacing the block‑diagonal structure in Orthogonal Finetuning with a butterfly factorization?
questions.question_body: In the paper, OFT uses a block‑diagonal orthogonal matrix to limit trainable parameters but this introduces expressivity issues. The authors then propose BOFT which factors a dense orthogonal matrix into a product of butterfly matrices. I’m confused about why a butterfly structure is expected to be more expressive yet still keep the number of parameters low. How does the butterfly topology enable dense connectivity while maintaining sparsity compared to the block‑diagonal approach?

questions.title: How does the information‑transmission view formalize the construction of a dense orthogonal matrix?
questions.question_body: Section 3 introduces an information‑transmission framework where multiplying several sparse matrices corresponds to sequential communication on a $d 	imes (m+1)$ grid. I understand the analogy qualitatively, but I cannot see how this perspective translates into concrete sparsity constraints on each factor $ m{B}_i$. Could someone walk through an explicit mapping from a butterfly factorization to an information graph and explain why each node eventually has a path to every other node?

questions.title: "Cayley parameterization" – how is it applied to each butterfly component?
questions.question_body: The paper says that each butterfly component $	ilde{ m{B}}^b(d,k)$ must be orthogonal, and one can enforce this by Cayley transform. For a $2 	imes 2$ block, it’s straightforward, but for larger blocks (e.g., $b=4$) or higher‐level butterfly factors ($k>2$), how exactly do we parameterize them with skew‑symmetric matrices? Is there a closed‑form representation for the non‑zero elements, or do we treat each $2b	imes 2b$ subblock independently?

questions.title: What does "effective trainable parameters" mean in BOFT($m,b$) and why is it $(b-1)dm/2$?
questions.question_body: The algorithmic description states that BOFT($m,b$) uses $ rac{1}{2}(b-1)d m$ effective trainable parameters when finetuning a $d	imes n$ layer. The paper mentions that elements that must be $ igl\pm1 igr/$ in any $d	imes d$ orthogonal matrix with only one non‑zero per row/column are not counted. How does this counting work across all butterfly components? A step‑by‑step derivation would clarify this.

questions.title: Why is multiplicative dropout used in BOFT instead of standard dropout?
questions.question_body: BOFT multiplies many orthogonal matrices in succession, and the authors propose a "multiplicative dropout" that sets chosen butterfly components or their sub‑blocks to identity during training. How does this differ from applying dropout to activations or weights as in LoRA? What effect does turning part of the butterfly factorization into an identity have on the overall orthogonality and expressivity?

questions.title: "Expressivity of BOFT"—does a larger $m$ always mean better approximation of any orthogonal matrix?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 states that BOFT is more expressive than OFT with the same block size and that by multiplying many pairs $ m{B}_{i,j}$ and their transposes one can approximate all orthogonal matrices. However, empirical results (Figure 6) suggest diminishing returns for large $m$. Why doesn’t increasing $m$ further always reduce approximation error? Is there an inherent limit due to the fixed sparsity pattern of butterflies?

questions.title: How does BOFT preserve the spectral norm of pretrained weights compared to LoRA?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that both OFT/BOFT multiply an orthogonal matrix from the left, thus preserving singular values. Is this property preserved when we use multiple butterfly components multiplied together? Does the product of several orthogonal matrices remain orthogonal? If yes, does it still guarantee identical spectral norms after finetuning?

questions.title: "Identity initialization" for BOFT—does initializing skew‑symmetric matrices at zero guarantee $ m{R}=I$ for all components?
